description: The **blockchain** invented a ledger that no one can forge alone. That idea opened the way to a whole new digital economy.

hero.hook: An account book that nobody owns, and that thousands of computers keep watch over together.

blocks.text: Imagine an account book that nobody owns alone, kept up to date at the same moment by thousands of computers all over the world, and almost impossible to forge. That is the starting idea of the **blockchain**, a technology often reduced to its first application, **Bitcoin**.
By letting people exchange value without going through a bank, this invention created a whole parallel economy, caught between promises of financial freedom and harsh criticism of its energy bill.

At the heart of the blockchain sits a simple idea: the **distributed ledger**. A bank keeps its accounts on its own servers. A blockchain instead relies on a network of [[peers]], thousands of computers that each hold an identical copy of every transaction.

The very first block of the Bitcoin blockchain, known as the “genesis block,” carried a hidden message: the front page of a British newspaper from January 3, 2009, about the state bailout of the banks. A political wink from its creator.

Each transaction is checked by the network, then bundled with others into a **block**. That block is tied to the one before it by a mathematical operation called [[hashing]], a kind of unique digital fingerprint. The result is an unbroken chain of blocks, hence the name blockchain. Changing a single old transaction would mean recalculating the whole chain and convincing more than half the network, which is close to impossible at this scale.

sections.title: A ledger that nobody controls alone

blocks.text: **Bitcoin**, launched in **2009** by a person (or a group) who stayed anonymous under the name [[Satoshi Nakamoto]], proved that a monetary system could work without a central bank. To guarantee scarcity, its creator set a hard ceiling: there will never be more than **21 million bitcoins**, much as gold is limited on Earth.

blocks.caption: Every transaction is checked by a network of computers before it joins the chain

blocks.text: In 2015, a second generation of blockchain arrived with **Ethereum**. Its big innovation: **smart contracts**. These are programs that run by themselves as soon as a condition is met: an automatic refund when a train is late, for example, with no middleman involved.

sections.title: Bitcoin and Ethereum: from payment to program

blocks.text: The success of cryptocurrencies comes with problems. The most debated one is the **energy use** of the Bitcoin network: its yearly electricity bill now matches that of an entire country such as Argentina.
The market also suffers from extreme **volatility**: the price of Bitcoin can swing 10% or 20% in a few hours. That instability keeps it, for now, from becoming a real everyday currency.

Finally, the relative anonymity of transactions has sometimes served illegal activity. Yet a blockchain is in fact completely transparent: the authorities can follow the flow of money, which makes laundering harder than in the classic world of cash.

Cryptocurrencies are now leaving the margins and entering traditional finance. Large banks offer to hold digital assets for their clients, and several states are thinking about issuing their own official digital money, a **[[CBDC]]** (central bank digital currency).

**Stablecoins**, cryptocurrencies whose price is pegged to a reserve of dollars or euros, act as a bridge between the two worlds. Beyond finance, sectors such as luxury goods (to fight counterfeiting), logistics (to track containers) and health care (to secure medical records) are adopting blockchain for its reliability.
In 2021, El Salvador became the first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender alongside the US dollar, obliging every merchant with the technical means to accept it.

Created in 2009, the blockchain is a shared ledger that is almost impossible to forge, and the supply of bitcoins is capped at 21 million units. It laid the groundwork for a new digital economy that institutions are now absorbing.
